metadata.title: How to Select Flanged Tubing Assemblies: Sealing, Port Matching and Installed Validation
metadata.seoTitle: Flanged Tubing Assemblies: Selection and Port Matching | FOREACH
metadata.seoDescription: Compare HF, HF6, HFL and HFL6 flat-bottom fittings: materials, tubing sizes, dimensions and nose clearance. Check M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF ports and define assembly validation.
metadata.coverAlt: FOREACH flanged tubing assemblies with different fittings and formed tube ends

deck: Select tubing material, ID and OD, both end fittings, backing washers, port geometry and installation dimensions together. Confirm that the flange is correctly compressed against the flat-bottom port, then specify retainers, labels and installed validation.

leadBlocks.text: In analytical instruments and automated fluid paths, tubing assemblies connecting pumps, valves and fluidic modules must meet sealing, routing and replacement needs as well as transport fluid. Making a connection is only part of the task: the tube flange, backing washer and receiving port determine whether compression acts at the intended sealing surface.

For existing flanged interfaces, check the original assembly and port drawings first. For a new OEM fluid path, define the configuration around routing, port spacing and maintenance. The following sections cover assembly structure, materials and dimensions, fitting selection and installation checks.

leadBlocks.alt: FOREACH flanged tubing assemblies and their end connections
leadBlocks.caption: Flanged tubing assemblies. Select fittings, tubing and end configurations to match the actual fluid path and equipment interfaces.

sections.title: What makes up a flanged tubing assembly, and how does it seal?

blocks.text: The preformed tube end has an outward-facing flange. During assembly, the threaded fitting applies axial force through a matched backing washer, supporting and compressing the flange against the sealing face of a compatible flat-bottom port. Check thread engagement and face sealing separately: a fitting that screws into a port does not necessarily seat the flange against its bottom.

blocks.alt: Position of the standard flat-bottom fitting, backing washer and tube flange
blocks.caption: HF standard flat-bottom fitting assembly: the washer sits between the fitting nose and the tube flange. The 20.5 mm overall length, 8.2 mm head diameter and 2 mm nose clearance shown apply to HF. See the four-series comparison below.

blocks.text: HF, HF6, HFL and HFL6 flat-bottom fittings are available for flanged tubing assemblies. HF and HFL have standard heads; HF6 and HFL6 are compact types. All use matched washers to compress the tube flange, but head dimensions, overall length, bores and nose geometry differ. Select a specific series and model; one set of dimensions cannot represent every fitting.
A complete preassembled unit can also include retainers and tubing labels. Identify each part’s function before deciding which options to include in the delivery drawing.

blocks.text: The O-ring or retaining sleeve behind the fitting limits sliding; it is not the receiving port’s seal. If the end interfaces differ, confirm the fittings and washers independently rather than assuming an identical configuration at both ends.

sections.title: How should tubing material, fitting material and tubing size be specified?

blocks.text: Start with fluid identity, concentration, operating temperature, contact time and cleaning procedure. FOREACH flanged assemblies offer FEP and PTFE tubing; fitting bodies and washers have their own material and size ranges. The body material does not identify all wetted materials in an assembly: determine the actual fluid-contact surfaces from its structure.

rows: Confirm chemical compatibility and suitability for the flanging process separately
Check the material, thread and tubing OD combination for the specific model
Select the specific thread, tubing OD and color configuration
Listed M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF versions use PPS; the listed small 6-40 UNF version uses PEEK
Do not transfer material specifications between different threads and sizes
SUS stainless steel, PEEK or PTFE, depending on size
Check ID, OD and thickness; not every size is available in every material

blocks.alt: Examples of PEEK, PVDF and PPS flat-bottom fitting bodies
blocks.caption: Examples of body materials. Color indicates appearance; confirm material from the model and delivery documentation. One material may be available in different colors.

blocks.text: Specify tubing ID, tubing OD and fitting through-bore separately. ID and length affect flow resistance and internal volume; OD determines the fit with the fitting, washer and forming tool. The fitting bore must provide suitable clearance for the selected tubing OD. Calling all three “tube diameter” is ambiguous.

The current assembly documentation lists tubing ODs of 1.6, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 and 3.2 mm. Specify ID and OD as a pair. For example, 0.8 × 1.6 mm in the configuration diagram means ID × OD, not two compatible tubing ODs. Match the pair to the selected material and forming requirements.

Chemical resistance alone does not make every wall thickness suitable for the same flanging process. Confirm the tooling, material and ID/OD range before forming; inspect end integrity and the flow passage afterward. Define the length datum in the drawing, such as the distance between sealing faces, to avoid confusing cut length with finished assembly length.

sections.title: How do HF, HF6, HFL and HFL6 flat-bottom fittings compare?

blocks.text: All four series offer M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF configurations. Check thread, tubing OD and material first, then compare head diameter, axial length and nose geometry. Dimensions below follow the series drawings linked on the website, in mm. They exclude the tube flange and washer and are not the exposed length after installation.

blocks.title: HF: standard head, three tubing OD groups

blocks.text: HF has an 8.2 mm head diameter, 20.5 mm overall length and a 2 mm unthreaded nose. The three tubing OD groups—1.6–2.0, 2.5 and 3.0–3.2 mm—have drawing bore sizes of 2.2, 2.7 and 3.4 mm respectively. Select PEEK, PVDF or PPS by model, and check turning clearance around the head and tubing exit space behind it.

blocks.title: HF6: a narrower and shorter compact alternative to HF

blocks.text: HF6 has a 6.4 mm head diameter and 17.6 mm overall length, respectively 1.8 mm and 2.9 mm smaller than HF. Its tubing groups, body materials and 2 mm nose clearance match the corresponding HF configurations. Consider HF6 for closely spaced ports or limited axial space, then check actual spacing, access for tightening and removal. Compact dimensions do not imply a higher pressure rating.

blocks.title: HFL: shorter body with a wider head

blocks.text: HFL has a 10 mm head diameter, 16.5 mm overall length and 1 mm nose clearance. It is axially shorter than HF but has a wider head. Check axial and radial space separately near housings or closely spaced ports. Website drawings list natural and black PVDF versions for tubing ODs of 1.6, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 and 3.2 mm individually; do not apply HF’s three-group sizing.

blocks.title: HFL6: slim body requiring checks of radial spacing and axial clearance

blocks.text: The HFL6 M6 and U28 drawings specify a 6 mm head diameter, 20 mm overall length and PPS body. It is narrower than the other three but longer than HF6 and HFL: “compact” does not mean smallest in every direction. These drawings do not identify a 2 mm unthreaded nose like HF/HF6. Check port compatibility against HFL6’s own geometry.

For HFL6 tubing ODs of 1.6, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 and 3.2 mm, nominal drawing bore sizes are 1.8, 2.2, 2.7, 3.2 and 3.4 mm respectively. The smaller HFL6-U40-16-PK-N uses a 6-40 UNF thread and PEEK body for 1.6 mm tubing OD. Confirm its installation dimensions separately; the M6/U28 dimensions in the table do not apply.

blocks.title: Turn a fitting choice into an assembly specification

items: Check the full equipment-port thread specification and flat-bottom sealing geometry before selecting the series. M6 and U28 models are not interchangeable.
Select by actual tubing OD and check bore size and tolerance. The fitting bore accommodates the tubing; it is neither tubing ID nor assembly flow-path diameter.
Use head OD to check interference between adjacent fittings. Use overall length, installed depth and tube exit direction to check axial space, allowing room for operation.
Match washer material, ID, OD and thickness to the fitting, tubing and port; confirm where the flange is supported and compressed.

blocks.text: The website’s standard and compact ferrule-fitting filters refer to other connection structures. The four flat-bottom series here are HF, HF6, HFL and HFL6; the four filter categories are not four flanged-assembly options. When replacing an assembly, check the series prefix, drawing revision and port geometry together.

sections.title: Why can an assembly leak even when the fitting screws into the port?

blocks.text: First check the complete thread specification. M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF are different; similar appearance or a few turns of engagement do not establish compatibility. Then check the shape, depth and condition of the port bottom to confirm that it provides the intended sealing contact.

For the flat-bottom flanged connections shown, the receiving port needs a sealing face that meets the drawing. An incompatible conical bottom can prevent seating and create leakage or local retention. Fitting nose geometry, washer thickness and flange dimensions jointly determine the assembled position; check for interference before effective compression is reached.

blocks.alt: The illustrated fitting’s 2 mm unthreaded nose clearance
blocks.caption: The HF/HF6 nose clearance is 2 mm; HFL is 1 mm. HFL6 M6/U28 drawings do not identify the same feature. These fitting dimensions must not be used as receiving-port internal-thread machining dimensions.

blocks.text: These clearance requirements belong to the corresponding assembly and port design; they are not a universal machining standard for all flanged fittings. When connecting to an existing valve body or fluidic module, provide a receiving-port section drawing rather than only a thread designation.

sections.title: How can part defects be distinguished from installation problems?

blocks.text: Check interfaces and parts before adjusting the assembly. Repeatedly increasing tightening force can permanently deform a plastic flange and conceal port mismatch. Follow the installation method and torque requirements for the specific fitting, tubing and assembly; do not use one value for every model.

blocks.alt: Close-up of two assembly ends showing fitting noses, washers and flanges
blocks.caption: Inspect how the flange, washer and fitting nose fit together. The photograph illustrates structure; sealing must still be verified under specified conditions.

items: Check fitting model, tubing OD, washer specification and receiving-port drawing to rule out mixed parts.
Inspect the flange for skew, cracks or deformation, and check whether forming or compression has affected the flow passage.
Check for missing, incorrect or damaged washers, and scratches or foreign matter on the port sealing face.
Assemble using the specified method; watch for tube twisting as the fitting turns.
Restore the actual routing, remove insufficient-length tension, tight bends and side loads, then retest under equipment conditions.

blocks.text: If an assembly passes on the bench but leaks after installation, prioritize routing and external loads. If the problem is concentrated at one port, check that end’s component combination and sealing face first. This helps distinguish interface mismatch, part condition and routing effects.

sections.title: What installed validation should samples undergo?

blocks.text: A static sealing check covers only its assembly and test conditions. For instrument use, validate the actual tubing length, routing and duty cycle, and include acceptance conditions in the delivery requirements.

rows: Length datum, components at both ends, port spacing, tool access and installed bends
Sealing under actual positive or negative pressure, temperature and pressure changes
Changes to tubing, flanges and sealing after exposure to actual reagents and cleaning fluids
Disassemble and reconnect using equipment-defined methods and cycle counts; inspect flanges, washers and sealing afterward
Check materials, dimensions, appearance, identification and test records against the agreed drawing

blocks.text: Define test pressure, duration, allowable leakage and reconnection cycles from equipment requirements and the confirmed assembly. A fitting or tubing component rating is not automatically a pressure, life or reuse guarantee for the complete assembly.

sections.title: What information is needed for a custom flanged tubing assembly?

blocks.text: When submitting requirements to FOREACH, designate the two ends as A and B and list each fitting, thread, washer and port requirement. Single- or double-ended flanging, tubing length, retainers and labels can be specified for the project; deliverable combinations follow the approved drawings and product documentation.

items: Fluid: reagent and cleaning-fluid names, concentrations, temperatures, contact times and operating mode.
Tubing: FEP or PTFE, ID × OD, color, finished length and measurement datum.
Ends A/B: fitting series, material, complete thread specification, washer requirements and receiving-port drawings.
Installation: routing, port spacing, bending space and maintenance/removal method.
Identification: retainers if required, label content, print orientation and installation position.
Acceptance: dimensional tolerances, appearance, cleanliness, operating sealing and maintenance/reconnection checks.

blocks.text: For replacement projects, include photographs of the original assembly and describe the problem, such as insufficient length, difficult installation, leakage after maintenance or batch variation. Relating the problem to structure and operating conditions helps determine whether to change tubing, fittings, washers or manufacturing and assembly requirements.

cta.title: Need to match a flanged tubing assembly to your equipment?
cta.description: Provide tubing material, ID × OD, finished length, both fittings and port drawings, together with fluid, temperature, pressure, retainer and labeling requirements to define candidate configurations and validation.
